question: Where was Frederick Douglass born?

gold.quote: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland.
Frederick Douglass was born in slavery as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey near Easton in Talbot County, Maryland.

question: To whom was Douglass hired out for a year to be broken?

gold.quote: He resolved to put me out, as he said, to be broken; and, for this purpose, he let me for one year to a man named Edward Covey.

question: After his mistress stopped teaching him, how did Douglass go on learning to read?

gold.quote: The plan which I adopted, and the one by which I was most successful, was that of making friends of all the little white boys whom I met in the street.

question: Who suggested the surname Douglass, and what had he just been reading?

gold.quote: Mr. Johnson had just been reading the “Lady of the Lake,” and at once suggested that my name be “Douglass.”

question: Which book did Douglass read that contained a dialogue between a master and his slave?

gold.quote: Just about this time, I got hold of a book entitled “The Columbian Orator.” Every opportunity I got, I used to read this book. Among much of other interesting matter, I found in it a dialogue between a master and his slave.

question: What trade was Douglass put to learn at Mr. Gardner's shipyard?

gold.quote: I was put there to learn how to calk.

question: How much did Douglass earn per day as a caulker?

gold.quote: I was now getting, as I have said, one dollar and fifty cents per day.

question: Whom did Douglass marry after reaching New York?

gold.quote: “This may certify, that I joined together in holy matrimony Frederick Johnson[3] and Anna Murray, as man and wife, in the presence of Mr. David Ruggles and Mrs. Michaels.
In 1838 he escaped from slavery and went to New York City, where he married Anna Murray, a free colored woman whom he had met in Baltimore.

question: Who tried to keep a Sabbath school for slaves in St. Michael's?

gold.quote: While I lived with my master in St. Michael’s, there was a white young man, a Mr. Wilson, who proposed to keep a Sabbath school for the instruction of such slaves as might be disposed to learn to read the New Testament.

question: According to Paine, what is government even in its best state?

gold.quote: Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one; for when we suffer, or are exposed to the same miseries by a government, which we might expect in a country without government, our calamity is heightened by reflecting that we furnish the means by which we suffer.

question: Why did Paine think it unnatural for Britain to rule America, judging by their size?

gold.quote: Small islands not capable of protecting themselves, are the proper objects for kingdoms to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.

question: How does Paine describe William the Conqueror?

gold.quote: A French bastard landing with an armed banditti, and establishing himself king of England against the consent of the natives, is in plain terms a very paltry rascally original.--It certainly hath no divinity in it.

question: How did Paine justify the cost of building a fleet?

gold.quote: A navy when finished is worth more than it cost.
It is the best money we can lay out.

question: According to Paine, now that debate has failed, what will decide the quarrel with Britain?

gold.quote: Arms, as the last resource, decide the contest; the appeal was the choice of the king, and the continent hath accepted the challenge.
By referring the matter from argument to arms, a new æra for politics is struck; a new method of thinking hath arisen.

question: Who was Massanello?

gold.quote: ¹ Thomas Anello, otherwise Massanello, a fisherman of Naples, who after spiriting up his countrymen in the public market place, against the oppressions of the Spaniards, to whom the place was then subject, prompted them to revolt, and in the space of a day became king.

question: What did Franklin get for three pence at a bakery when he first arrived in Philadelphia?

gold.quote: He gave me, accordingly, three great puffy rolls.

question: What was Franklin's club of mutual improvement called?

gold.quote: I should have mentioned before, that, in the autumn of the preceding year, I had form'd most of my ingenious acquaintance into a club of mutual improvement, which was called the Junto;[54] we met on Friday evenings.

question: Whose book persuaded the young Franklin to stop eating meat?

gold.quote: When about 16 years of age I happened to meet with a book, written by one Tryon, recommending a vegetable diet.

question: Which virtue came first in Franklin's list of thirteen, and what was its precept?

gold.quote: 1. Temperance. Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.

Temperance first, as it tends to procure that coolness and clearness of head, which is so necessary where constant vigilance was to be kept up, and guard maintained against the unremitting attraction of ancient habits, and the force of perpetual temptations.

question: What precept did Franklin attach to humility?

gold.quote: Imitate Jesus and Socrates.

gold.quote: Another stroke of his oratory made me asham'd of that, and determin'd me to give the silver; and he finish'd so admirably, that I empty'd my pocket wholly into the collector's dish, gold and all.

gold.quote: And now I set on foot my first project of a public nature, that for a subscription library.

question: Under what pen name did Franklin write letters for his brother's newspaper?

question: What does Wollstonecraft say girls are taught from infancy about beauty?

gold.quote: Taught from their infancy, that beauty is woman's sceptre, the mind shapes itself to the body, and, roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adorn its prison.

question: Which writers on female education does Wollstonecraft accuse of making women weaker and more artificial?

gold.quote: I may be accused of arrogance; still I must declare, what I firmly believe, that all the writers who have written on the subject of female education and manners, from Rousseau to Dr. Gregory, have contributed to render women more artificial, weaker characters, than they would otherwise have been; and, consequently, more useless members of society.

question: What does Wollstonecraft think of Rousseau's character Sophia?

gold.quote: I now principally allude to Rousseau, for his character of Sophia is, undoubtedly, a captivating one, though it appears to me grossly unnatural; however, it is not the superstructure, but the foundation of her character, the principles on which her education was built, that I mean to attack; nay, warmly as I admire the genius of that able writer, whose opinions I shall often have occasion to cite, indignation always takes place of admiration, and the rigid frown of insulted virtue effaces the smile of complacency, which his eloquent periods are wont to raise, when I read his voluptuous reveries.

question: Why does Wollstonecraft argue that permanent armies are bad for liberty?

gold.quote: A standing army, for instance, is incompatible with freedom; because subordination and rigour are the very sinews of military discipline; and despotism is necessary to give vigour to enterprises that one will directs.

question: Where did Mary Wollstonecraft believe she was born?

gold.quote: Her father was so great a wanderer, that the place of her birth is uncertain; she supposed, however, it was London, or Epping Forest: at the latter place she spent the first five years of her life.

question: Which author did Wollstonecraft renew her acquaintance with in 1796?

gold.quote: In 1796 she revived or improved an acquaintance which commenced years before with Wm. Godwin, author of "Political Justice," and other works of great notoriety.

gold.quote: Über dem Tisch, auf dem eine auseinandergepackte Musterkollektion von Tuchwaren ausgebreitet war -- Samsa war Reisender --, hing das Bild, das er vor kurzem aus einer illustrierten Zeitschrift ausgeschnitten und in einem hübschen, vergoldeten Rahmen untergebracht hatte.
